content.title: About
content.content: Peas and carrots cooked by boiling are a popular side dish and a staple in soups and stews. Peas are a legume rich in protein and fiber, while carrots are a root vegetable packed with beta‑carotene, vitamin A and antioxidants.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Peas belong to the legume family and are among the oldest cultivated crops used by humans.
Carrots were originally purple; the orange variety was developed in the 17th century in the Netherlands.
The pea‑carrot combination appears in traditional dishes worldwide, such as the British “pea and carrot mash” and the Russian “мутная каша”.
Boiling retains most of the vitamin C in peas, while heat improves the bioavailability of beta‑carotene in carrots.
Both vegetables are easy to grow in temperate climates; peas fix nitrogen in the soil, and carrots improve soil structure.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: Cooked peas provide about 5 g of protein per 100 g, making them valuable for vegetarian diets.

items.title: Supports eye health
items.content: Carrot beta‑carotene converts to vitamin A, essential for vision and immune function.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Both vegetables supply soluble and insoluble fiber, promoting healthy digestion and cholesterol balance.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Vitamins C and E, along with carotenoids in carrots, help neutralize free radicals.

items.title: Blood‑sugar regulation
items.content: Pea fiber slows glucose absorption, and the low glycemic index of the combo helps maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to peas, ranging from skin rash to severe anaphylaxis.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Peas contain phytates, which can reduce mineral absorption when consumed in very large amounts.

items.title: Possible pesticide residues
items.content: Non‑organic peas and carrots may carry pesticide residues; thorough washing before cooking is recommended.

items.title: Excess beta‑carotene
items.content: Very large intakes of carrots can cause carotenemia—a harmless yellowing of the skin.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve peas and carrots as a side dish, add them to soups, stews, salads, or casseroles. After boiling, they can be lightly sautéed for a crisp texture. Enjoy plain, lightly salted, or with a pat of butter.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked peas and carrots in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 3–4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags; they retain flavor and nutrients for up to 6 months.
